newsitem.title: USA: ABN AMRO chair sees no big buys.
newsitem.headline: ABN AMRO chair sees no big buys.

text.p: The chairman of Dutch banking group ABN AMRO Holding NV said Wednesday the bank would focus on growing internally in the United States without major acquisitions being planned.
"There is no need for us to do anything except internal growth," the executive, Peter Jan Kalff, told reporters.
He also said the bank, the 14th-biggest in the world, would continue to concentrate on its Midwest market in the United States.
"The Midwest is a highly attractive commercial banking market," said Kalff, who was in New York to mark the opening of ABN AMRO's American Depositary Receipts (ADRs) on the New York Stock Exchange.
"It is not the sort of boom-bust economy we have witnessed here in the Northeast, in New England with the real estate problems, or in California or in Texas."
ABN AMRO is the biggest foreign bank in the United States, with $86 billion in assets and 11 branches concentrated in the Midwest.
It completed the $1.9 billion purchase of Michigan's Standard Federal Bancorp this month and finished buying Chicago Corp, an investment bank, in January.
"With the acquisition of Chicago Corp we are very hopeful that we can really broaden the franchise further by combining commercial banking and investment banking," he said.
"We want to be the universal bank that ABN AMRO has always been."
Asked if ABN AMRO would be interested in buying a regional bank the size of Ohio's Banc One Corp, with $101.6 billion in assets, Kalff said, "Probably not."

He said Banc One was too big and buying it would distort ABN AMRO's operations worldwide. "If we would focus exclusively on the Midwest or the United States we would lose our balance" geographically, he said.
ABN AMRO's ADRs were trading at 18-5/8 after being priced at 18-1/2. Volume in late afternoon was 3.9 million shares, putting the company eighth on the New York Stock Exchange's most-active list.
The bank offered 14 million ADRs representing an equal number of ordinary shares. The ADRs are about one percent of ABN AMRO's outstanding shares.
Kalff said the shares would help ABN AMRO carry out future acquisitions and avoid the extra taxes on shareholders when the bank paid cash for purchases.

He refused to comment about estimates of future earnings per share (EPS), saying U.S. securities laws barred him from doing so. Analysts have estimated 1997 EPS at 2.54 guilders, up eight percent from last year.
Asked if 1997 revenues or profits would be higher than last year's, Kalff said, "If you look at my face, then you can draw a conclusion. I'm a happy man."
